(b) IUPAC System

The systematic (IUPAC) nomenclature treats an alkyl halide as an alkane with a halo–substituent: Fluorine is fluoro–, chlorine is chloro–, bromine is bromo–, and iodine is iodo–. The result is a systematic haloalkane name. The following steps should be followed for naming alkyl halides.

1. Select the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms, containing the halogen atoms.

2. Number the chain from the end closer to halogen atom. If both alkyl and halogen are present in a molecule then number the chain from the end closer to alkyl group or halogen atom.

3. Indicate the position of halogen and alkyl group by suitable locants.

4. Prefix di, tri, tetra etc. is used to indicate the number of halogen atoms.

5. If two different halogen atoms are present in a molecule at same position from the two ends, the one to be assigned the lower locant is that one cited first in alphabetical order. When an alkyl and halogen occupy equivalent positions, again number the chain from the end to give lowest number to one that comes first in alphabetical order.

Examples

17.1.2 Structure of Alkyl Halides

To understand the structure of alkyl halides, let us consider methyl chloride as an example. In this molecule the carbon atom is sp³-hybridized and all the bonds of carbon are sigma. During the process of bond formation, one sp³–hybrid orbital of carbon atom overlaps with the half-filled p orbital of chlorine atom and form carbon-chlorine sigma bond, while the remaining three sp³-hybrid orbitals overlap with 1s orbitals of three hydrogen atoms and form three carbon-hydrogen sigma bonds (Figure 17.1). The bond lengths of carbon-chlorine and carbon-hydrogen bonds are 178 pm and 108 pm respectively. The H–C–H and H–C–Cl bond angles are approximately equal to 109.5°.

Figure 17.1 Orbital hybridization model of bonding in methyl chloride

17.1.3 Physical Properties

Lower alkyl halides such as methyl fluoride, methyl chloride, methyl bromide, ethyl fluoride, ethyl chloride and propyl fluorides are gases at room temperature. Mostly higher n-alkyl halides up to C₁₆ are liquids and above are solids.

They have higher boiling points than the corresponding alkanes. For a given alkyl group the boiling points of alkyl halides increase with increasing size of the halogen atom, while for a given halogen atom the boiling points of alkyl halides increase with the increasing size of the alkyl group. For isomeric alkyl halides, the compound with the more highly branched alkyl group normally has the lowest boiling point.

They are usually insoluble in water due to their inability to form hydrogen bonding with water. They are soluble in organic solvents.

Alkyl chlorides and alkyl fluorides are lighter than water while alkyl iodides and alkyl bromides are denser than water. A mixture of an alkyl halide and water separates into two layers. When the alkyl halide is a fluoride or chloride, it is the upper layer and water is the lower. The situation is reversed when the alkyl halide is a bromide or an iodide.

The two alkyl halides, n-propyl chloride and isopropyl chloride, given above are example of position isomers.

(b) IUPAC System

The systematic (IUPAC) nomenclature treats an alkyl halide as an alkane with a halo–substituent: Fluorine is fluoro–, chlorine is chloro–, bromine is bromo–, and iodine is iodo–. The result is a systematic haloalkane name. The following steps should be followed for naming alkyl halides.

1. Select the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms, containing the halogen atoms.

2. Number the chain from the end closer to halogen atom. If both alkyl and halogen are present in a molecule then number the chain from the end closer to alkyl group or halogen atom.

3. Indicate the position of halogen and alkyl group by suitable locants.

4. Prefix di, tri, tetra etc. is used to indicate the number of halogen atoms.

5. If two different halogen atoms are present in a molecule at same position from the two ends, the one to be assigned the lower locant is that one cited first in alphabetical order. When an alkyl and halogen occupy equivalent positions, again number the chain from the end to give lowest number to one that comes first in alphabetical order.

Examples

17.1.2 Structure of Alkyl Halides

To understand the structure of alkyl halides, let us consider methyl chloride as an example. In this molecule the carbon atom is sp³-hybridized and all the bonds of carbon are sigma. During the process of bond formation, one sp³–hybrid orbital of carbon atom overlaps with the half-filled p orbital of chlorine atom and form carbon-chlorine sigma bond, while the remaining three sp³-hybrid orbitals overlap with 1s orbitals of three hydrogen atoms and form three carbon-hydrogen sigma bonds (Figure 17.1). The bond lengths of carbon-chlorine and carbon-hydrogen bonds are 178 pm and 108 pm respectively. The H–C–H and H–C–Cl bond angles are approximately equal to 109.5°.

Figure 17.1 Orbital hybridization model of bonding in methyl chloride

17.1.3 Physical Properties

Lower alkyl halides such as methyl fluoride, methyl chloride, methyl bromide, ethyl fluoride, ethyl chloride and propyl fluorides are gases at room temperature. Mostly higher n-alkyl halides up to C₁₆ are liquids and above are solids.

They have higher boiling points than the corresponding alkanes. For a given alkyl group the boiling points of alkyl halides increase with increasing size of the halogen atom, while for a given halogen atom the boiling points of alkyl halides increase with the increasing size of the alkyl group. For isomeric alkyl halides, the compound with the more highly branched alkyl group normally has the lowest boiling point.

They are usually insoluble in water due to their inability to form hydrogen bonding with water. They are soluble in organic solvents.

Alkyl chlorides and alkyl fluorides are lighter than water while alkyl iodides and alkyl bromides are denser than water. A mixture of an alkyl halide and water separates into two layers. When the alkyl halide is a fluoride or chloride, it is the upper layer and water is the lower. The situation is reversed when the alkyl halide is a bromide or an iodide.
